01 · SUMMARY

The problem, and where to start

 

Air India Group reported a consolidated loss of ₹22,238 crore for FY26 in its regulatory filings. The loss is more than twice the FY25 loss. The group's income fell about 9%, and its expenses rose.

Four external events hit Air India in the same year.

1.    Pakistan closed its airspace to Indian airlines.

2.   The Iran war closed more airspace in West Asia.

3.   Jet fuel prices rose.

4.   The rupee weakened against the dollar.

 

A product team cannot reopen an airspace or set the price of jet fuel. A product team can decide where the airline earns its money. It can lower the cost of serving each passenger. It can also make each passenger stay loyal for longer. I would start in four places.

1           Rebuild the long-haul network around southern hubs, and win back connecting passengers from the Gulf. Air India can fly west from Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Chennai with little need for Pakistan's airspace. Kochi, Coimbatore, Madurai, Mangaluru and South India's other international airports would feed those hubs. Travellers would then connect in India instead of in Dubai or Doha. This is the Emirates hub-and-spoke model, adapted to India.

2           Handle disruption automatically. The system rebooks each passenger before the passenger calls. The system also refunds and compensates the passenger where the rules require it.

3           Redesign the booking flow and extras around India's new free-seat rule. Air India would replace seat fees with bundles and upgrade bids. It would also sell seats that would otherwise fly empty as a cheaper Light fare, with no checked bag and no meal.

4           Move AI from answering questions to taking actions. Air India would apply AI to service first, and then to pricing and maintenance.

EXPECTED IMPACT

I estimate that the four product ideas, plus loyalty, are worth roughly ₹1,700–2,900 crore a year once fully running. This estimate is illustrative, and section 4 shows the working. The network change is the larger prize. However, I cannot size it without route-level data. Together, these ideas close part of the gap, not all of it. Air India fully controls each of them.

 

02 · CONTEXT

Where Air India stands

 

Tata Group took over Air India in January 2022. In September 2022, Air India launched Vihaan.AI, a five-year transformation plan. The plan targets at least 30% of the domestic market. It also targets better service, reliability and technology. Air India merged with Vistara on 12 November 2024. Air India then moved Club Vistara's roughly 4.5 million members into a single programme, Maharaja Club.

THE HEADWINDS

Since 2025, Air India has faced the below headwinds. Most of them sit outside the airline's control.

1.    Pakistan's airspace closure. Pakistan has barred Indian airlines from its airspace since April 2025, and Pakistan renews the ban every month. The latest notice runs to 24 November 2026. Air India estimated that the closure costs it about $455–600 million a year in extra fuel and crew time. Foreign airlines are not covered by the ban, so they still offer shorter flights between India and Europe or North America.

2.   Crude oil and jet fuel. The US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February 2026 and disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. On 1 April 2026, India's state oil companies raised the Delhi price of jet fuel for international flights by 114.5%, to a record ₹2,07,341 per kilolitre. The government shielded domestic flights from most of that rise. Fuel now makes up more than half of the group's operating costs, according to reports on its results.

3.   West Asia disruption. The Iran war also closed airspace across West Asia. According to reports on Air India's FY26 results, that region carries about 16% of Air India's capacity.

4.   The weak rupee. Air India pays for aircraft leases and much of its fuel in dollars, but it earns much of its revenue in rupees. The Federation of Indian Airlines said in April 2026 that the rupee had fallen to its lowest level in six years. Air India's foreign-exchange loss rose to ₹7,388 crore in FY26, from ₹1,545 crore a year earlier.

5.   The AI171 crash. On 12 June 2025, Air India flight AI171, a Boeing 787-8 bound for London Gatwick, crashed shortly after take-off from Ahmedabad and killed 260 people. In July 2026, the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau told the Supreme Court that it expected its draft final report in October 2026. Until that report is public, the crash keeps Air India's safety record under scrutiny.

6.   Pilots, training and fatigue. In July 2025, DGCA issued four show-cause notices to Air India that cited 29 violations, including pilots who did not receive their mandatory weekly rest. Reuters reported that a separate DGCA audit that month found 51 safety lapses, including gaps in pilot training and the use of unapproved simulators. DGCA's stricter duty-time rules took full effect in November 2025, so every Indian airline now needs more pilots for the same schedule.

7.    Fleet and supply chain. Air India is refitting its older aircraft under a $400 million programme. Air India has finished the 27 older A320neos, but its seat suppliers are late. Air India now expects to finish the last 777-300ERs in October 2028. Its maintenance costs rose to ₹14,976 crore in FY26.

 

Figure 1. The headwinds that hit Air India between April 2025 and April 2026. Sources: Gulf News, AAIB statements to the Supreme Court, Reuters via Dawn, Tribune India, Free Press Journal and regulatory filings.

WHAT IS IMPROVING

Air India's punctuality has improved, but Air India still trails IndiGo. DGCA data for June 2026 puts the group's domestic on-time performance at 85.9%, against 89.4% for IndiGo. In May 2026, the gap was wider, at 74.5% against 82.8%. On international flights, Cirium ranked Air India fourth in the world for punctuality in June 2026.

Air India also has a new chief executive. Tewolde Gebremariam, who previously ran Ethiopian Airlines, took charge on 1 October 2026. He has set up a cost committee.

Air India already owns one strong digital asset. Its AI assistant, AI.g, handles about 40,000 queries a day. Microsoft reports that AI.g has resolved more than 13 million conversations. AI.g passes only 3% of queries to a human agent.

04 · RECOMMENDATIONS

Strategy first, then product by product

 

Figure 3. Schematic, not to scale. Positions are approximate and show the network logic only. The 85% figure is from Business Standard, June 2025.

STRATEGY

A southern hub-and-spoke network

Largest prize · needs route data

THE PROBLEM

Air India runs most of its long-haul network from Delhi. The airspace ban hurts Delhi more than any other Indian city.

Air India also loses many connecting passengers to Gulf airlines. Business Standard reported in June 2025 that about 85% of Indian travellers who need a connection, roughly 17 million passengers, change planes at a foreign hub on a foreign airline. Most of them connect in Dubai or Doha.

THE EMIRATES LESSON

Emirates flies every route through one hub, Dubai. Its short routes feed the hub, and the hub fills its long-haul aircraft.

In 2025–26, Emirates carried 53.2 million passengers. It made a record pre-tax profit of $6.2 billion in the same year.

India cannot copy Dubai's state backing or its cost base. Air India can copy the discipline, which means sending each aircraft where it earns the most.

WHAT I WOULD BUILD

I would build a southern network that lets travellers connect in India instead of the Gulf. The network works in the below way.

1.    Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Chennai act as long-haul gateways, because their routes west barely touch Pakistan's airspace. Mumbai plays the same role on the west coast.

2.   South India's other international airports feed those gateways. These include Kochi, Thiruvananthapuram, Kozhikode and Kannur in Kerala, Coimbatore, Madurai and Tiruchirappalli in Tamil Nadu, and Mangaluru in Karnataka.

3.   Air India and Air India Express also feed the gateways from Delhi, Lucknow, Jaipur and other northern cities.

The product work is the connection itself. The connection product meets the below conditions.

1.    The passenger holds one ticket for the whole trip.

2.   The system checks bags through to the final destination.

3.   If the first flight is late, the system rebooks the passenger on the next connection.

WHY PASSENGERS WOULD SWITCH

Today, a traveller from Kochi to London usually changes planes in Dubai or Doha. In this network, the same traveller changes planes in Bengaluru, and Air India keeps the whole fare.

The passenger saves money only under the below conditions.

1.    Air India prices the one-stop Indian connection below the Gulf airlines' fare.

2.   The domestic first leg adds little to Air India's cost per passenger.

3.   The total journey time stays close to the Gulf route.

Air India controls the first condition directly. I would test the other two with route-level data.

THE POLICY TAILWIND

The government supports this direction. In 2026, it moved to develop Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru as international transit centres. Civil Aviation Minister Ram Mohan Naidu has said that roughly 35% of India's departing international passengers transit through foreign hubs.

The Iran war also showed passengers the risk of depending on Gulf airports.

TWO HONEST LIMITS

Air India studied a refuelling stop in Mumbai or Ahmedabad for its Delhi to North America flights. In June 2026, Air India said that payload studies favoured a corridor over Mongolia instead. A stop that only refuels the aircraft does not pay. A hub pays, because new passengers board there.

For some southern cities, an Indian connection adds distance. Kochi to London through Bengaluru flies slightly further than through Dubai, so Air India has to win on price and convenience.

HOW I WOULD MEASURE IT

I would track the below measures.

1.    The share of southern India's connecting passengers who connect in India instead of the Gulf.

2.   The misconnection rate at each gateway.

3.   Revenue per long-haul flight from each southern gateway.

4.   Market share won back from foreign airlines on India to Europe routes.

The Navi Mumbai airport supports this plan. When Air India moves Air India Express flights to Navi Mumbai, it frees slots at Mumbai's main airport for long-haul connections.

 

PRODUCT

Disruption handling and refunds

₹150–300 cr a year · illustrative

THE PROBLEM

When Air India cancels a flight, passengers phone, queue and wait. DGCA data shows that refunds made up about a fifth of passenger complaints in several months of 2025.

DGCA's refund rules from 26 March 2026 shorten the refund timelines. A slow refund is now a regulatory risk as well as a reputational one.

WHAT I WOULD BUILD

When a disruption happens, the system rebooks the passenger before the passenger asks. The system then sends a WhatsApp or push message with the below choices.

1.    Accept the new flight.

2.   Take a refund.

3.   Take a voucher.

The passenger chooses with one tap. If the DGCA rules require compensation, the system calculates the amount and pays it automatically.

HOW I WOULD MEASURE IT

I would track the below measures.

1.    The share of disrupted passengers who resolve the problem without a human.

2.   The median time to a refund.

3.   Repeat bookings by disrupted passengers within 90 days.

The value comes from fewer calls and fewer penalties. Retained loyalty is the bigger prize, but I cannot size it from outside.

 

PRODUCT

Booking flow and extras

₹600–900 cr a year · illustrative

THE PROBLEM

DGCA now requires airlines to keep at least 60% of seats free to select. The rule removes part of a reliable fee.

The Federation of Indian Airlines has warned that airlines will raise base fares to make up the loss. A higher base fare would hurt Air India's headline price.

WHAT I WOULD BUILD

I would replace single fees with bundles that fit the trip. For a family flying Delhi to London, the system offers seats and bags together. For a business traveller, the system offers lounge access and flexibility.

I would add upgrade bids for premium seats that would otherwise fly empty. I would also measure every step of the booking flow, because no outsider can see the drop-off rates.

HOW I WOULD MEASURE IT

I would track the below measures.

1.    Revenue from extras per passenger.

2.   Conversion at each booking step.

3.   Take-up of each bundle.

A 1% lift on ₹71,870 crore of income is worth about ₹700 crore a year.

 

PRODUCT

Light fares for unsold seats

₹200–400 cr a year · illustrative

THE PROBLEM

DGCA data shows that the Air India Group filled between about 79% and 84% of its domestic seats in several months of 2025 and 2026. Every empty seat still costs Air India fuel, crew and airport charges, but it earns nothing.

Air India's cheapest fare still includes services that many price-sensitive travellers do not need. Air India announced in October 2024 that even its Value fare on Europe and UK routes includes a 23 kg checked bag.

WHAT THE RULES ALLOW

DGCA allowed zero-baggage fares in February 2021. The same circular allowed airlines to unbundle meals, seat selection and other services, and to charge for them on an opt-in basis.

Air India can therefore sell a cheaper fare that leaves out the checked bag and the meal.

WHAT I WOULD BUILD

I would release a Light fare only for seats that the forecast says will fly empty. The Light fare follows the below rules.

1.    The passenger travels with cabin baggage only.

2.   The fare includes no meal or drink, except water.

3.   The system assigns the seat at check-in, unless the passenger pays to choose one.

4.   The passenger can add a bag or a meal later, at a fixed price.

The system opens the Light fare only close to departure, and only when the forecast shows unsold seats. This rule protects the full fares that most passengers already pay.

HOW THE FARE SCREEN WORKS

The booking screen shows every fare side by side. The screen marks each service with a clear tick or cross, as Figure 4 shows.

The passenger sees what the Light fare leaves out before paying. This stops surprise baggage charges at the airport, which are a common source of complaints.

HOW I WOULD MEASURE IT

I would track the below measures.

1.    The load factor on flights where the Light fare is open.

2.   Revenue per flight, against similar flights without the Light fare.

3.   The share of Light-fare buyers who would otherwise have paid a full fare.

4.   Complaints about baggage charges at the airport.

Suppose the Light fare fills one extra seat in every hundred, at about 60% of the average fare. That adds roughly 0.6% to income, or about ₹430 crore a year. Some Light-fare buyers would otherwise have paid a full fare, so I use a lower range of ₹200–400 crore. This estimate is illustrative.

 

Figure 4. Proposed fare screen, illustrative. The Light fare appears only on flights that the forecast says will have empty seats.

PRODUCT

Maharaja Club

₹200–400 cr a year · illustrative

THE PROBLEM

Air India merged two loyalty programmes in 2024. CardAdvisor reports that Air India then revalued the Maharaja Club award chart on 1 April 2026.

If members feel that their points have lost value, they book with other airlines.

WHAT I WOULD BUILD

The system shows each member a clear, personal view of what their points can buy. I would grow point earning through co-brand cards and Tata Group brands.

The system sends targeted offers to members on the routes that the detours hit hardest.

HOW I WOULD MEASURE IT

I would track the below measures.

1.    Partner revenue.

2.   The share of bookings from active members.

3.   Churn among top-tier members.

Partner revenue is the main lever, but I cannot see the contracts.

 

DATA

Crew and fleet scheduling

Protection against a very bad month

THE PROBLEM

In December 2025, IndiGo misjudged how many pilots it needed under DGCA's new duty-time rules. Dataful's analysis of DGCA data shows that IndiGo paid ₹22.76 crore in cancellation compensation that month.

That is about four times what IndiGo paid in the previous eleven years. Air India was far less affected, but the lesson applies to every airline.

WHAT I WOULD BUILD

Before Air India publishes a schedule, the planning tool tests the schedule against the below conditions.

1.    The DGCA duty-time rules.

2.   Expected sick leave.

3.   The weather season.

On the day of a disruption, the tool suggests the crew and aircraft swaps that cancel the fewest flights.

HOW I WOULD MEASURE IT

I would track the below measures.

1.    Cancellations caused by crew shortages.

2.   The cost of each disruption.

3.   The time to recover the network.

 

AI

From answers to actions

₹550–900 cr a year · illustrative

THE PROBLEM

AI.g answers questions well, but answering is the easy part.

Most of the value lies in completing tasks for passengers. More value lies in decisions that passengers never see.

WHAT I WOULD BUILD

I would build in the below three stages.

1.    AI.g completes tasks, such as changing a flight or adding a bag.

2.   Pricing models forecast demand by day and choose each day's long-haul routing.

3.   Maintenance models predict part failures from aircraft data.

HOW I WOULD MEASURE IT

I would track the below measures.

1.    Tasks completed per conversation.

2.   Unit revenue against forecast.

3.   Unplanned technical delays.

A 1% gain in yield is worth about ₹700 crore a year.

 

Figure 5. Illustrative annual value ranges for the five product ideas, about ₹1,700–2,900 crore in total. I have not sized the network strategy or the scheduling tool, because both depend on internal data.

05 · ROADMAP

Twelve to eighteen months, in three phases

 

I have ordered the phases deliberately. AI models need clean, connected data, so I place the platform work before the AI work. I start the network change with a study, because a hub would be expensive for Air India to undo.

Figure 6. Proposed roadmap. I have coloured each bar by its workstream. The text under each phase says how I would know that the phase worked.

06 · HONESTY

Risks and what I would need to check

 

I wrote this case study from outside the airline, so much of it rests on assumptions. Before I build anything, I would want answers to the below questions.

1.    Which routes, by origin and destination, would fill long-haul flights from a southern hub.

2.   What a southern hub would cost Air India in slots and ground handling.

3.   Whether Air India can price an Indian connection below the Gulf airlines and still earn a profit.

4.   How many Light-fare buyers would otherwise have paid a full fare.

5.   The real drop-off rates in the booking flow.

6.   Current revenue from extras per passenger, and how much of it the free-seat rule removed.

7.    The true cost of disruption today, including compensation, hotels and call-centre time.

8.   How far the merged systems of Air India, Vistara and Air India Express share data.

9.   Which of these ideas Air India already has under way. Air India may be ahead of me on several.

 

A NOTE ON NUMBERS

Every value in this piece is illustrative. A real business case replaces each value with internal data. I expect several of the values to move.
